title: Heartbeat-prefetch deadlock + OOM retrospective
content:
Summary:

Small cascade on 2025-10-26 that manifested as intermittent request stalls and pod OOM kills across two serving pools (eu-west-1 and us-west-2). Root pattern: a race between the KV cache heartbeat/TTL renewal and the prefetch worker's eviction/compaction code produced a mutex deadlock combined with continuous-batching inflight growth, which led to unbounded memory pinned by KV entries and eventually OOMs.

Why this doc exists:
- Capture the on-call timeline and ad-hoc mitigations (what we did to stop customer impact).
- Surface short-term mitigations and a prioritized list of long-term fixes.
- Draft a concise runbook excerpt for on-call handling of similar cache/deadlock SREs.

Impact observed:
- ~0.8% of requests returning 502/504 during the 03:30-04:45 UTC window on 2025-10-26 for two clusters.
- P90 token latency increased from ~120ms to ~1.8s for affected routes.
- Memory RSS growth on worker pods from baseline 6GB -> 12GB over ~40 minutes prior to OOM kill.
- 7 pods OOMKilled (across 2 deployments), autoscaler added replacement pods; customer impact reduced after mitigations.

Immediate timeline (UTC):
- 2025-10-26 03:28: alert: high kv_cache_pinned_bytes on eu-west-1-serving-*.
- 2025-10-26 03:32: on-call paged (pagerduty), SRE channel created (#sre-incident-2025-10-26).
- 03:33: metrics: queue depth for continuous-batcher increased; p99 latency rising.
- 03:40: first pod OOMKill observed in eu-west-1.
- 03:45: mitigation 1 applied: scaled serving pool +2025: set serving-runtime flag --kv-prefetch=disabled on k8s deploy (rollout via kustomize) to stop background prefetch workers.
- 03:52: temporary drop in p99 latencies, but memory still climbed on surviving pods in us-west-2.
- 04:10: mitigation 2: increased kv_cache_eviction_interval from 30s -> 10s and forced compaction via admin endpoint /admin/kv/compact on affected pods.
- 04:20: traffic normalized; no further OOM kills after compaction completed.

Root cause analysis (hypothesis from debugging session):
- Several interacting pieces:
  1) Heartbeat TTL renews for large prefix-based entries when requests reference cached prefixes. There was a regression in the heartbeat code (PR merged 2025-10-20) that changed ordering of lock acquisition during TTL update.
  2) Prefetch worker (async background prefetch + compaction) attempts to remove expired entries and compact the index. During heavy continuous-batching, many requests pinned transitive KV entries while holding per-request read locks.
  3) The changed heartbeat ordering meant a background compaction path and the request path could use overlapping locks in different order -> classic deadlock possibility. On load, a small number of threads ended up deadlocked waiting on each other.
  4) Deadlock blocked eviction progress; continuous-batcher kept accepting requests (bounded by batch size but large parallelism), causing the effective pinned memory footprint to grow (lots of entries could not be evicted).
  5) Fragmentation and pinned pages prevented kernel page reclamation -> OOM kills.

Evidence that supports hypothesis:
- Thread dumps (pstack/gdb) from two pods showed stack traces waiting in kv::Lock::acquire and kv::Compactor::run, each holding the other lock (attached stacks saved to S3).
- Admin metrics: kv_cache_ringed_evictions decreased to near-zero during the incident while kv_cache_pinned_entries and kv_cache_pinned_bytes spiked.
- The problematic code revision is referenced in PR 1029 (linked above). Bisect to commit X (commit sha: abcdef123456) reproduces locally under stress harness (see infra/serving-runtime/e2e/kv-lock-race).

Repro steps (local stress):
- Checkout commit abcdef123456 (branch: playing/kv-lock-race)
- Start dev-serving with --continuous-batching enabled and prefetch worker flag enabled.
- Run the stress scenario: python tests/stress/kv_lock_race.py --concurrency 120 --seq-len-dist heavy --prefix-hotspots 80%.
- Observe thread deadlocks via gdb -p <pid> and metrics stepping as above.

Short-term mitigations applied (in order taken):
1) Disable prefetch workers globally for affected pools (--kv-prefetch=disabled) to break compaction path.
2) Force compact/evict on impacted pods via /admin/kv/compact.
3) Temporarily increase heap limit on node pool (k8s node pool size bump) to reduce OOM frequency while fixes are deployed.
4) Rollback the heartbeat ordering change (revert of commit abcdef123456) in an emergency hotfix and canary it to one pool.

Notes on mitigations: disabling prefetch stopped the compaction path that was acquiring locks in the conflicting order; compact call unblocked eligible entries and reclaimed memory. Rolling back the heartbeat change removes the ordering inversion and is the primary code blocker.

Long-term fixes (prioritized):
- P0: Fix lock ordering in heartbeat update path and add stress test that induces the race (owner: Samir, ETA: 2 days). PR#1029 is the basis; update and land after local stress passes.
- P0: Add a hard cap on per-request pinned KV memory and fail fast if a request would exceed it (owner: Rina, ETA: 1 week).
- P1: Add background watchdog that detects low eviction throughput + high pinned bytes and toggles prefetch to read-only mode (non-destructive) or signals autoscaler.
- P1: Add e2e test that runs continuous-batching + heavy prefix hot-spot traffic for 30m in CI nightlies.
- P2: Improve metrics and alerts: create alert for kv_cache_pinned_bytes > 10GB for 5m, and combined alert if kv_cache_ringed_evictions < 1/min while pinned_bytes rising (owner: Diego).

Runbook excerpt (for on-call):
- Symptoms: alerts for kv_cache_pinned_bytes, p99 latency > 1s on generation routes, pod OOMKilled.
- Triage steps (fast):
  1) Check Prometheus: kv_cache_pinned_bytes, kv_cache_total_entries, kv_cache_ringed_evictions, continuous_batcher_queue_depth, generation_p99_latency.
  2) kubectl get pods -n serving -l app=serving-runtime -o wide, find OOMKilled. kubectl describe pod <pod> to see OOM event.
  3) Exec into healthy pod, hit /admin/metrics and /admin/kv/stats. curl -s http://localhost:8080/admin/kv/stats | jq .
  4) If pinned_bytes high and evictions near-zero, disable prefetch via kustomize overlay: set env KV_PREFETCH=disabled, rollout.
  5) If memory continues to climb, trigger /admin/kv/compact on affected pods.
  6) If still failing, scale the deployment up by 20% to absorb load and reduce per-pod pressure.
  7) Pager escalation: notify eng-serving-runtime and on-call infra lead.

Commands we used (examples):
- kubectl -n serving get pods -l app=serving-runtime -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.phase}'
- kubectl -n serving exec -it <pod> -- sh -c "curl -sS localhost:8080/admin/kv/stats | jq ."
- kubectl -n serving set env deploy/serving-runtime KV_PREFETCH=disabled --record
- curl -X POST http://<pod>:8080/admin/kv/compact
- pstack <pid> > /tmp/pstack-<pod>.txt (for linux stacks)

Post-incident actions and owners: (short bullets)
- Samir: land lock-ordering fix + unit test (ETA 2025-11-05).
- Rina: implement per-request pinned memory cap + regression test (ETA 2025-11-12).
- Diego: create alert rules and a Prometheus dashboard tile for pinned_bytes vs ringed_evictions (ETA 2025-11-04).
- Priya: run a tabletop with SRE + serving-runtime + infra to walk through the runbook and refine wording (ETA 2025-11-07).

Open questions / discussion points we left in the retro:
- Should prefetch be redesigned to operate as a best-effort read-only cache with no compaction authority (compaction left to a single controller)? Pros/cons? (Rina to prototype).
- Is there a way to make kernel reclaim behavior less harmful (madvise/madvise-like strategies) without impacting latency? (Systems team follow-up).
- How aggressive should autoscaler respond to early signals (pinned bytes) vs conventional CPU/memory thresholds?

Appendix: quick links + artifacts we generated during debugging:
- thread dumps: s3://redwood-dumps/sre/2025-10-26/
- local reproducible harness: infra/serving-runtime/tests/stress/kv_lock_race.py
- PR (hotfix): https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1029
- Incident timeline slack export: https://slack-exports.redwood/sre-2025-10-26

Notes to future on-call: keep this file as the canonical short-retro. If you're reading this as a new on-call, the immediate heuristics are: if pinned_bytes climbs and evictions drop -> disable prefetch + compact. Don't immediately scale down; scaling up + compact wins time for a proper rollback.

End of notes.
